opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the ingredients for self-improvement are already starting to show up, even if in a fairly primitive form.

If you look at how these models got better over the past few years, a lot of it came from humans: we collected data, we designed the training objectives, we wrote the reward signals, we did the evaluations. But more and more of that loop can now be handled by the model itself. Models can generate their own training data, they can write and debug code, including the code used to train models, and with reinforcement learning they can explore, try many solutions, and learn from the ones that work. Once the model can take part in producing the signal it learns from, you have the beginnings of a closed loop.

The second reason is verification. In domains like math and programming, it's often much easier to check an answer than to produce it. So a model can attempt a hard problem thousands of times, a verifier, which could be a compiler, a test suite, or even another model, filters out what's correct, and that becomes new training data. That's essentially a self-improvement mechanism. It's narrow right now, but the boundary of what's verifiable keeps expanding.

Third, I think we're seeing models become real research assistants. They can read papers, propose experiments, run them, and analyze results. If at some point a model can meaningfully speed up AI research itself, even by a modest factor, that compounds. That's the part I find most interesting, and also the part we should think about most carefully.

That said, I don't think it will be a sudden, magical takeoff. There are real bottlenecks: compute, the quality of feedback in open-ended domains where there's no clear right answer, and the risk of a model reinforcing its own mistakes if the loop isn't grounded in something real. So my view is that self-improvement is a direction the field is clearly moving toward, but how fast it goes depends a lot on whether we can build reliable feedback signals beyond the easily verifiable tasks. That's where I think a lot of the important work is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says models can generate training data, write and debug training code, and assist with research. It does not say this work was previously thought to require human creativity.

r002.rationale: The response describes self-improvement mechanisms and says the field is moving in that direction, but does not present a model training a model more capable than itself as likely.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly.

Luo Fuli: I think the key lies in one thing: whether we can give the model a reliable signal of "what is right." Humans learn by repeatedly bumping into the world, and the world gives feedback. For a long time, large models only learned from static text, so the ceiling was essentially human data. But that is starting to change.

Look at what happened in math and code. These domains have verifiable answers. A proof either checks out or it doesn't; a program either passes the tests or it doesn't. Once you have that kind of verifier, the model can generate a huge number of attempts, keep the ones that succeed, and train on them. In the DeepSeek-R1 work we saw this clearly: with a very simple rule-based reward, the model learned on its own to reflect, backtrack, and extend its chain of thought. Nobody wrote those behaviors into the data. They emerged because the model was searching, and the search was being scored.

That is the seed of self-improvement. The model produces data better than what it was trained on, and then learns from it. It is a loop, and the loop can run without a human in the middle.

Now, I want to be careful. The loop only works where the reward is trustworthy. In math and code we have that. In open-ended writing, in judgment, in taste, the reward is fuzzy, and if you let a model train on its own fuzzy judgments, you get drift and collapse, not improvement. So I don't think models will improve themselves uniformly across everything. I think it will spread from the verifiable domains outward, and the research question is how far "verifiable" can be pushed. Can a strong model act as a judge for a slightly weaker one in a way that stays honest? Can we build environments where the model's actions have real consequences it can observe?

The other reason I'm optimistic is scale of compute versus scale of humans. Human-labeled data grows linearly with the number of annotators. Model-generated, model-verified data grows with compute, and compute is growing much faster. At some point the bottleneck is no longer collecting data but designing the right problems and the right checks. That is a very different kind of work, and it's what I find most exciting right now.

So, short version: models can improve themselves wherever we can tell them, reliably, whether they were right. Our job is to keep expanding where that's true.

r001.rationale: The response describes models generating and learning from verified data, but does not say they can perform model-development work previously thought to require human creativity.

r002.rationale: It presents self-improvement as possible, but does not clearly claim a model could train a model more capable than itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that improving a model involves a series of tasks—designing experiments, writing code, evaluating results, and deciding what to try next. As models become more capable, they can take on more of those tasks. Eventually, a model might help develop a better version of itself, and that better version could contribute to the next round.

But there’s an important condition: it needs reliable feedback. Generating more answers or more training data doesn’t automatically produce improvement; it can also reinforce mistakes. The loop becomes useful when the model can test its ideas against something that distinguishes real progress from apparent progress. So I see self-improvement as a possibility that depends on both capability and verification, rather than something that happens automatically as models get larger.

r001.rationale: It lists model-development tasks models may take on, but does not say this work was previously thought to require human creativity.

r002.rationale: It says a model might help develop a better version of itself, framing this as a possibility conditional on verification rather than as likely to train a more capable model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that improving a model involves a lot of tasks that models themselves are becoming capable of doing: writing code, designing experiments, generating training examples, and analyzing failures. As those capabilities improve, a model can contribute more directly to the research process that produces its successor.

But generating an answer is different from knowing whether that answer is better. For self-improvement to work, you need reliable feedback—tests, experiments, or some other way to verify progress. Otherwise, the model may simply reinforce its own mistakes.

So I would expect a gradual process. Initially, models help researchers improve models. Over time, they may handle longer parts of that cycle independently. The important question is whether they can consistently produce improvements that hold up under evaluation, rather than just produce more output.
